subject: Business Models
title: Platform Breakups
description: A fast breakdown of Platform Breakups for builders.

hook.text: The US government sued to break up Standard Oil in 1911. Could it do the same to Meta or Google?

buildup.text: Proposals include unwinding Meta's acquisitions of Instagram and WhatsApp to restore competition.

discovery.text: AT&T's 1984 breakup created competition that drove phone prices down and innovation up.

twist.text: Platform breakups may not work like industrial ones. Splitting a network in half destroys its value.

climax.text: The debate continues: are platform monopolies natural and efficient, or anticompetitive and harmful?

punchline.text: Split a network, destroy the value. Breaking up platforms is harder.

quiz.question: Why might breaking up a platform be different from breaking up an industrial monopoly?
options: Splitting a network destroys its core value

details.summary: Platform breakups are structural remedies where regulators force dominant technology companies to separate their integrated business units into independent companies. Proposals have targeted separating Amazon's marketplace from its retail, and Google's search from its ad business.
details.whyItMatters: Breakup proposals represent the most extreme regulatory intervention in platform economics. Whether they restore competition or destroy value through lost integration benefits is the defining debate in tech antitrust policy.
takeaways: Structural separation divides integrated platform empires into independent units
Proposals target conflicts of interest like Amazon competing with its sellers
Breakups are the most extreme and controversial antitrust remedy available

faq.question: What platform breakups have been proposed or attempted?
faq.answer: The US DOJ sought to break up Google's search and ad businesses. Congress proposed separating Amazon's marketplace from its private label business. The FTC sought to unwind Meta's acquisitions of Instagram and WhatsApp. None have been completed as of 2026.

faq.question: Would breaking up big tech platforms benefit consumers?
faq.answer: Proponents say it would restore competition and innovation. Opponents argue that integration creates consumer value through seamless experiences and that separated units would provide worse products. The empirical evidence is limited since no major platform breakup has occurred.
